transcript.content: Hi, I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, Dr. Smith, I... I suppose I'm here because my husband insisted, but honestly, it’s about the kitchen. It started—oh, it must be nearly two years ago now. We hired this contractor, a man named Gary, to redo the cabinets and the countertops, and I thought it would be a simple job, you know? Just a few weeks. But almost immediately, things started going wrong, and not just normal wrong. I’m talking about deliberate things. Like the hinges on the upper left cabinet being slightly off-center, just enough so the door doesn't close flush. And then I started noticing him talking to the neighbors. Mrs. Gable across the street, and that young couple two doors down. They’d stand at the end of the driveway, whispering. 

And now, for almost two years, I’ve been absolutely sure—I mean, I know it in my bones—that Gary and some of the people on my block are quietly working together. They’re conspiring to cheat us. They want to keep my kitchen half-wrong on purpose. It’s like a game to them! My husband, bless his heart, he tries to tell me I’m imagining things. He pulls out all these receipts and invoices, pointing at dates and materials, and Gary always has some excuse ready—supply chain issues, backordered parts, humidity affecting the wood. But I know better. You don't just accidentally order the wrong shade of grout three times in a row while simultaneously having hushed conversations with the neighborhood busybody, do you? They’re doing it on purpose, doctor, and no amount of paperwork my husband waves in my face is going to change what I see happening right in my own home.
Aside from what you've told me about Gary and the neighbors, have you ever heard voices, or seen or sensed things that other people around you don't seem to notice?

Voices? Oh, heaven's no. No, no, no. I know exactly what you're getting at with a question like that, Dr. Smith, and I can assure you, my mind is as sharp as a tack. I don't hear phantom voices whispering in the walls, and I certainly don't see things that aren't right there in front of my very own eyes. 

My husband—well, sometimes I honestly think he wishes I *was* just hearing things, because then it would be easy for him, wouldn't it? Then he could just pat my hand and say it's all in my head. But I only hear what is actually, truly being spoken out loud in the real world. Like last Tuesday, for instance. I was out front watering the petunias—they've been looking just dreadful with this dry spell we've been having, I've had to soak them twice a day—and I heard, plain as day, Gary's heavy diesel truck pull up. And I didn't just imagine the sound of his boots crunching on the gravel, or the way he deliberately lowered his voice to a mumble when that young man from two doors down walked over with his dog. 

That is real life, doctor, not some... some imagination or whatever it is you're looking for. My hearing is perfectly fine, maybe even too good for my own good, because I catch the things they think I'm missing. So, no, I don't see ghosts or hear the television talking to me or any of that nonsense. I just see a poorly installed tile backsplash and hear the very real sound of people scheming to take advantage of a retired couple.

Before this situation with Gary and the neighbors started about two years ago, have you generally had a long-standing pattern of distrusting or suspecting the motives of people in your life—friends, family, coworkers—or is this kind of intense suspicion something new and specific to this kitchen situation?

Oh, no, no, no. Nothing like this, Dr. Smith. I mean, well, I've always been a careful person, you understand. You have to be careful in this world, especially nowadays. When my husband and I were both working—I worked as a receptionist at a dental office for thirty-two years, Dr. Henderson's office, maybe you know him? He retired back in '15, wonderful man, very particular about his appointment book, which I appreciated. But anyway, I was always the one who made sure the bills were paid on time, that the bank statements matched up. You know, just sensible things. I never thought people were out to get me. I had lovely friends at the office, and we'd do potlucks on Fridays. I made a wonderful potato salad, the secret is just a dash of celery seed, not too much mayonnaise. 

So, no, I wasn't going around thinking my coworkers were plotting against me or anything silly like that. I trusted my friends, I trusted my family. My sister Elaine and I, we've always been close, even though she lives all the way out in Ohio now and we mostly just talk on Sunday evenings. But this thing with Gary? This is entirely different. It's so specific, you see. It's not just a general feeling of, oh, people are bad. It's *him*. And it's that kitchen. Before he walked into our house with his muddy boots and his tape measure, I was perfectly content. I spent my days gardening, doing my crosswords, volunteering at the library bake sale—I always brought my lemon bars, they were a big hit. I never had a reason to look out the front window and wonder what the neighbors were whispering about, because they weren't whispering about anything that concerned me! 

But then the cabinets arrived, and the hinges were wrong, and the grout was the color of dirty dishwater instead of the 'Alabaster White' we agreed on. And that's when it all shifted. That's when I had to start paying attention, because if I didn't, who would? My husband certainly wasn't going to; he just wants peace and quiet and to watch his golf tournaments on the weekends. So, to answer your question, doctor, no. I have never been a suspicious woman. I've been a sensible woman. But when someone is practically flashing a neon sign that says they're trying to pull the wool over your eyes, well, you'd have to be a fool not to notice, wouldn't you?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a fixed, non-bizarre delusional belief (persecutory/conspiracy theme involving a contractor and neighbors) that has persisted for approximately two years. There are no hallucinations (auditory or visual), no disorganized speech, no negative symptoms, and no evidence of mood episode overlap. The delusion is circumscribed to this specific situation rather than pervasive, and premorbid functioning was normal with no long-standing paranoid personality traits (she reports trusting friends/family, stable 32-year work history, social engagement). Insight is absent regarding the delusion, but reality testing is otherwise intact, and daily functioning (gardening, crosswords, volunteering) is preserved outside the delusional system. This presentation is most consistent with Delusional Disorder, Persecutory Type (F22.0), distinguishing it from Schizophrenia (no hallucinations/disorganization) and Paranoid Personality Disorder (no long-standing pervasive distrust predating the specific stressor).
